A Satellite Foundation Model Maps Addis Ababa's Informal Settlements — and Finds a Heat Penalty Hidden Until Nightfall (2017–2024)

Author: Nazma Chowdhury Status: Draft (70 hand-digitized labels; daytime + nighttime thermal analysis)

Abstract

Every recent study of Addis Ababa's urban heat island relies on hand-crafted spectral indices (NDVI/NDBI) and linear or geographically-weighted regression, and none is framed around informal-settlement inequity. I take a different approach: classifying urban fabric directly from AlphaEarth Satellite Embeddings — Google's 64-dimensional learned representation of the Earth's surface at 10 m — with a shallow per-pixel probe trained on hand-digitized labels, and relating the result to Landsat surface temperature (LST). Trained once on 2024 labels and applied to 2017 and 2024, the linear probe separates informal from formal fabric at grouped cross-validated AUC 0.938 and maps clear settlement expansion at the city's peri-urban fringe. Contrary to the guiding hypothesis, informal fabric is not hotter: after controlling for vegetation and elevation, it is slightly cooler in daytime LST (−0.41 °C in 2017, −0.38 °C in 2024), a result robust to linear, quadratic, and elevation-matched controls, and stable over time (class×year interaction +0.03 °C, p = 0.20). I then extend the analysis to nighttime with MODIS thermal data — and the picture inverts. The daytime cooling disappears after dark: in 2017 informal fabric is significantly hotter at night (+0.30 °C per-pixel; +1.13 °C in a purity-restricted 1 km-cell test, p ≈ 10⁻¹¹), and a core-vs-fringe decomposition shows the nocturnal penalty concentrates in the established dense core (+0.34 °C, p = 0.06) while the newly-expanded fringe shows none. The daytime null was therefore an artifact of the proxy: daytime land-surface temperature hides a heat penalty that is real at night, when dense fabric releases stored heat and residents cannot cool down. The learned-embedding classifier is a clear methodological advance over index-based mapping and generalizes to the expansion frontier that administrative-boundary studies exclude; the day-vs-night contrast is the substantive contribution.

1. Introduction

Urban heat is an equity problem: the residents least able to adapt often live where thermal load is highest. Addis Ababa is urbanizing rapidly, and its informal settlements are expanding into the peri-urban fringe. A cluster of 2024–2026 studies quantifies the city's heat island, but all stop at spectral-index regression and none isolates an informal-settlement term or asks whether an equity gap is emerging over time.

This project asks: can a satellite foundation model detect informal fabric and any associated thermal signal — without hand-crafted indices — and track how it changes as settlements expand? The contributions are:

  1. The first use of a satellite foundation model (AlphaEarth) for Addis Ababa fabric classification.
  2. A confounder-adjusted estimate of the informal-vs-formal LST difference, with a train-once/apply-twice design for an honest 2017→2024 trend.
  3. A daytime-vs-nighttime comparison showing the heat penalty is invisible by day but present at night — a direct, empirical demonstration of why time-of-day choice determines whether urban-heat inequity is detected at all.
  4. A core-vs-fringe decomposition locating that nocturnal penalty in the established dense settlement rather than the expanding frontier.

2. Related Work

Existing Addis heat-island work uses NDVI/NDBI with OLS or geographically-weighted regression, or splits results by urban-morphology type via SPSS regression. None uses learned representations or an explicit informal-settlement inequity frame. AlphaEarth Foundations introduces the annual 10 m, 64-dimensional embeddings used here and shows that shallow probes on them match or beat task-specific models. Deprived-area machine-learning mapping in Accra/Lagos/Nairobi and a spatial-deprivation study of Addis inform where informal fabric concentrates.

3. Data

Layer Source Resolution Role
Land representation AlphaEarth Satellite Embedding V1 Annual 10 m, 64-dim Classifier input
Surface temperature (day) Landsat 8/9 C2 L2 ST (dry-season median) 30 m → 10 m grid Outcome
Surface temperature (day+night) MODIS Terra+Aqua LST (dry-season median) 1 km Outcome (extension)
Vegetation Sentinel-2 NDVI (dry-season median) 10 m Covariate
Elevation SRTM 30 m Covariate
Urban mask GHS-BUILT-S (2025 epoch) 100 m Study-area definition
RGB Sentinel-2 (B4/B3/B2) 10 m Visualization only

Study area. The FAO GAUL administrative boundary (~542 km²) is tighter than the built-up city and excludes the peri-urban expansion fringe — precisely where informal growth happens, and where 27% of my informal labels fell. I therefore define the study area as the administrative boundary buffered outward 10 km, then masked to built-up land (GHS-BUILT-S ≥ 500 m² per cell), yielding ~420 km² of urban fabric (5008×4956 pixels at 10 m). This keeps rural farmland from contaminating the "formal/other" class with cool non-urban pixels. All layers are dry-season (Dec–Feb) composites to avoid Ethiopia's rainy-season cloud.

4. Labels

No public informal-settlement shapefile exists for Addis. I hand-digitized 70 polygons (31 informal / 39 other) over 2024 high-resolution basemap imagery, spanning both the inner city and the peri-urban fringe, guided by literature-identified deprivation hotspots. Labels were drawn only against 2024 imagery; the classifier is applied unchanged to 2017 (Sec. 5). Sixty-four polygons fell on valid built-up pixels. Train/validation splits are by polygon, not pixel, so spatially-correlated pixels never straddle the split.

5. Method

Classifier. A per-pixel shallow probe on the 64-dim embedding, following AlphaEarth's evaluation protocol. Three models are compared under polygon-grouped 5-fold cross-validation: a linear probe (logistic regression), a small MLP, and gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost). Features are standardized on training folds only.

Train once, apply twice. The model is trained on 2024 labels and the frozen decision function is applied to both years' embeddings. Any 2017→2024 difference in output therefore reflects land-cover change, not labeling drift. Pixels flipping other→informal define the settlement-expansion map.

Statistics. For each year: Mann–Whitney U on LST by predicted class, and OLS LST ~ class + NDVI + elevation to isolate the fabric effect. A pooled LST ~ class×year + covariates model tests whether the gap changed. An elevation-matched cross-check compares classes within 50 m elevation bands.

Nighttime extension. I repeat the adjusted model with MODIS night LST (and MODIS day as a same-sensor control) as the outcome. Because MODIS is ~1 km and informal patches are often smaller, a cell frequently mixes classes; I therefore add a purity-restricted test using only 1 km cells that are ≥70% one class (the 10 m class map aggregated to the MODIS grid), and a core-vs-fringe decomposition that labels pure-informal cells as established core (already informal in 2017) or expansion (informal only by 2024) and compares each to other cells for 2024 night LST, adjusting for elevation and NDVI.

6. Results

Figure 1. The three data views for 2024. Left: Sentinel-2 true-colour. Centre: predicted fabric class (red = informal, grey = other) from the AlphaEarth linear probe. Right: dry-season Landsat surface temperature. The urban mask restricts analysis to built-up land; white is masked/out-of-boundary.

6.1 Classification

The linear probe is the strongest and least overfit, consistent with the AlphaEarth paper:

Model CV AUC CV F1 Per-polygon AUC
Logistic regression 0.938 0.853 0.935
MLP 0.896 0.831 0.912
XGBoost 0.861 0.770 0.856

Figure 2. Polygon-grouped cross-validated ROC. The linear probe (logistic regression, AUC 0.938) beats the MLP and gradient-boosted trees — the expected result for AlphaEarth embeddings, where shallow probes already capture the signal.

Predicted informal prevalence among built-up land rises from 31% (2017) to 42% (2024), and the change map flags 18% of valid pixels as other→informal expansion, concentrated at the peri-urban fringe — the qualitative pattern expected from Addis's growth.

Figure 3. Settlement change from the frozen classifier applied to both years. Red marks other→informal expansion, concentrated at the peri-urban fringe that the buffered study area was designed to capture; dark red is stable informal fabric.

6.2 Thermal difference by class

Contrary to the hypothesis, informal fabric is cooler, not hotter, in daytime LST:

Year Raw median ΔLST Adjusted (NDVI+elev) 95% CI Rank-biserial
2017 −0.76 °C −0.405 °C [−0.433, −0.376] 0.18
2024 −0.90 °C −0.379 °C [−0.406, −0.352] 0.25

Mann–Whitney rejects equal LST distributions in both years (p < 10⁻¹⁶⁰; note that the ~100k-pixel sample makes even small effects significant, so magnitude matters more than p). The effect is small.

Figure 4. The daytime result. Landsat LST distributions by predicted fabric class for each year (red = informal, blue = other). In both years the informal distribution sits slightly lower on the temperature axis — the opposite of the hypothesised heat penalty. Section 7 shows this reverses at night.

6.3 Robustness and trend

Informal sits ~113 m higher than other fabric (median 2450 vs 2337 m), so elevation is the prime confound. The cooler-informal effect survives every control: linear −0.379, quadratic −0.367, elevation-matched −0.303 °C. The pooled model shows no significant change 2017→2024 (class×year interaction +0.025 °C, 95% CI [−0.013, 0.064], p = 0.20). Per-elevation-band differences are heterogeneous — informal is clearly cooler in the lowest and highest bands but marginally warmer around 2300–2400 m — so the city-wide number is a modest average, not a uniform law.

7. Extension: does the penalty appear at night?

The daytime null (Sec. 6.2) has an obvious suspect — time of day. Urban-heat inequity is largely a nocturnal, heat-retention phenomenon: dense fabric with high thermal mass stores daytime radiation and releases it after dark, exactly when residents without cooling are exposed. Landsat only sees ~10:30 local. I therefore re-ran the adjusted analysis on MODIS night LST, with MODIS day as a same-sensor control.

The daytime cooling reverses at night. Landsat-day and MODIS-day agree almost exactly (both −0.45 °C in 2017), ruling out a cross-sensor artifact — and then the same MODIS sensor swings positive at night:

Year Landsat day MODIS day MODIS night day→night shift
2017 −0.445 °C −0.446 °C +0.298 °C +0.74 °C
2024 −0.380 °C −0.205 °C −0.075 °C +0.31 °C

In both years the informal effect moves toward hotter from day to night. In 2017 it crosses zero into a significant nighttime heat penalty (+0.30 °C, 95% CI [+0.27, +0.32]).

Figure 5. Adjusted informal-vs-other effect (°C) by source. Negative (orange/red) = informal cooler; positive (blue) = informal hotter. Daytime Landsat and MODIS agree that informal fabric is cooler; the same-sensor MODIS night bar reverses sign in 2017 and rises toward zero in 2024 — the signature of nocturnal heat retention.

The purity-restricted test sharpens 2017. Using only 1 km cells that are ≥70% one class, informal cells are +1.13 °C hotter at night than other cells in 2017 (95% CI [+0.80, +1.46], p ≈ 2×10⁻¹¹; 97 informal vs 947 other cells). The 2024 purity contrast is null (+0.03 °C) — which the next test explains.

Why 2024 washes out: core vs fringe. Splitting 2024 pure-informal cells by whether they were already informal in 2017 (established core) or appeared only by 2024 (expansion) and comparing each to other cells on 2024 night LST:

Group cells median elev (m) adjusted night Δ vs other 95% CI p
Core (established) 164 — +0.34 °C [−0.01, +0.69] 0.059
Expansion (new fringe) 60 — −0.14 °C [−0.67, +0.39] 0.60

Figure 6. 2024 nighttime heat penalty (adjusted, vs other cells) for established core informal versus the newly-expanded fringe. The core trends hotter at night (+0.34 °C, marginal at p = 0.06); the expansion fringe shows no penalty — consistent with newer, lower-density settlement not yet having developed the thermal mass that retains heat overnight.

The core effect is marginal (p = 0.06, 164 cells) and I do not overstate it, but its direction is clear and it dilutes to the observed 2024 null once the penalty-free expansion cells are mixed in. Taken together — a strong, significant 2017 night penalty and a core-concentrated 2024 signal — the nighttime evidence supports the reading that daytime LST simply could not see the heat burden.

8. Discussion

The headline is a twist with a resolution. By day, a strong classifier finds no heat penalty — informal fabric is even slightly cooler. But this is an artifact of the outcome variable, not the settlements. Landsat images the surface near 10:30 local, when dense, low-rise informal fabric with narrow alleys and small footprints sits in shade, while the "formal/other" class is dominated by hot open surfaces — industrial roofs, wide roads, bare lots. Switch the measurement to night, and the sign flips: informal fabric runs hotter (Sec. 7), most clearly in the established dense core where thermal mass has had time to accumulate. Daytime land-surface temperature is the wrong instrument for a phenomenon that is fundamentally nocturnal; the penalty was there all along, hidden by the time of the overpass. That the effect concentrates in the core rather than the expanding fringe is itself informative: the heat burden is a property of mature, consolidated informal fabric, and the frontier may be growing into it.

9. Limitations

  • LST ≠ air temperature. Both Landsat and MODIS measure surface temperature; neither is the air temperature residents breathe. The night result is the better proxy for lived exposure but still a proxy.
  • MODIS is coarse. At 1 km the night analysis mixes fabric types; the purity-restricted and core/fringe tests mitigate but cannot eliminate this, and the 2024 core effect is marginal (p = 0.06).
  • Resolution ceiling. 30 m (day) / 1 km (night) thermal vs. 10 m classification supports no per-building claim.
  • Self-digitized labels. 70 polygons, annotator judgment, no field survey; the target of 100–150 would firm the estimates (though the daytime direction is robust).
  • Correlational. Association after confounders, not mechanism.
  • Single city, single season. No automatic generalization; dry-season only.

10. Conclusion

Learned satellite embeddings classify Addis Ababa's informal fabric at AUC 0.94 and cleanly track its expansion — a real advance over index-based mapping, and one that reaches the peri-urban frontier administrative studies miss. The thermal story is the lesson: by day, informal fabric shows no heat penalty and even reads slightly cooler, but that is an artifact of the mid-morning overpass. At night the penalty emerges — informal fabric runs up to ~1 °C hotter, concentrated in the established dense core — exactly where heat harms residents who cannot cool down after dark. The methodological takeaway generalizes beyond Addis: whether urban-heat inequity is detected depends on the time of day you measure it, and daytime land-surface temperature can hide a penalty that is plainly there at night. Nighttime, and ultimately air-temperature, measurement is the necessary next step.
